4. DISCUSSÃO

Este manuscrito mostrou pela primeira vez que os extratos das flores de AH e
dos caules com folhas de MO inibiram as atividades proteolítica, coagulante
plasmática e PLA 2 do veneno de B. jararaca e B. neuwiedi, mas não conseguiram
inibir tais atividades do veneno de B. jararacussu. As SVMPs purificadas, bothropasina
e jararagina, do veneno de B. jararaca possuem atividade hemorrágica e alteram o
sistema de coagulação sanguínea; a miotoxicidade do veneno de B. jararacussu deve-
se à presença das PLA s2 bothropstoxina I e bothropstoxina II (Ayres et al., 2015).
Experimentos adicionais utilizando tais enzimas purificadas poderiam ser realizados
para abordar o mecanismo de ação dos extratos de AH e MO. Embora as espécies
avaliadas no presente trabalho pertençam ao mesmo gênero, a literatura tem
mostrado variações intra e interespecíficas dos venenos, inclusive de acordo com
dieta, sexo, idade e habitat entre os componentes biologicamente ativos dos venenos
(Queiroz et al ., 2008) . Assim, o desenvolvimento de um tratamento para
envenenamento usando moléculas ou extratos brutos de fontes naturais capazes de
neutralizar todas essas proteínas e peptídeos ativos é uma questão difícil.
Os efeitos antiofídicos dos extratos AH e MO contra as atividades dos venenos
in vitro foram bastante diferentes, provavelmente devido a pequenas variações entre
a composição química de ambos os extratos vegetais. Por exemplo, os compostos
hiperosídeo e ácido 3,4-di-hidroxibenzoico estão ausentes no MO, mas presentes no
AH em quantidades consideráveis (15,45 mg/kg e 29,54 mg/kg, respectivamente). O
hiperosídeo é uma molécula presente no extrato da planta Hypericum brasiliensis que
possui efeito antiofídico (Assafim et al., 2011). O composto quercetina também é um
constituinte do H. brasiliensis que possui uma ampla faixa de atividades
farmacológicas, incluindo anti -inflamatória, redução da insuficiência cardíaca e
anticâncer (Perazzo et al., 2008). No entanto, no trabalho conduzido por Assafim et
al., a quercetina não inibiu as atividades hemorrágica, letal e edematogênica do
veneno de B. jararaca como fez o extrato bruto do H. brasiliensis.
Assim, a inibição dos extratos AH e MO das atividades proteolítica e coagulante
dos venenos da B. jararaca e da B. neuwiedi pode não se dever apenas ao conteúdo

84

de quercetina, que é conhecida por se ligar a metais divalentes, como Ca² ⁺ e Zn²⁺,
que são cruciais para a atividade enzimática das PLA s2 e SVMPs, respectivamente.
Além disso, tais compostos das plantas são capazes de se ligar a aminoácidos do sítio
ativo de tais enzimas. No entanto, o conteúdo de quercetina nos extratos do H.
brasiliensis no trabalho de Assafim et al. (2011) não foi descrito, e o período de coleta
das plantas pode alterar o conteúdo de compostos e alterar a ação inibitória contra
toxinas dos venenos. Assim, essa falta de dados pode limitar a comparação entre os
resultados que descrevem o antiveneno de plantas.
Além disso, o composto apigenina- 7-O-glicosídeo está presente em baixa
quantidade no MO (28,83 mg/kg) e indetectável no AH e, portanto, a atividade
antiofídica não está relacionada a este composto; a quercetina- 3D-glicosídeo está
presente em ambos os extra tos, mas em quantidades maiores no MO. O extrato AH
possui 55 vezes mais do glicosídeo flavonoide astragalina do que o MO; e este
composto tem sido usado como modelo para desenvolver medicamentos contra
algumas doenças, incluindo obesidade, câncer, osteoar trite, osteoporose e diabetes
mellitus (Chen et al., 2023; Ruan et al., 2024).
Verificou-se que o método Soxhlet permite a preparação de amostras de extrato
com valores de pH praticamente neutros (pH do extrato MO – 6,95 ± 0,20; pH do
extrato AH – 6,23 ± 0,18) e é caracterizado por alta concentração de polifenóis.
Constatou-se que os extratos de AH e MO continham quercetina- 3D-glicosídeo nas
quantidades de 99,35 mg/kg e 62,65 mg/kg, respectivamente, e astragalina nas
quantidades de 8,76 mg/kg e 469,33 mg/kg, respectivamente. No entanto,
quantidades maiores de alguns compostos nos extr atos de AH e MO não estão
diretamente envolvidas na eficácia inibitória deles contra os efeitos tóxicos dos
venenos. Pode- se especular que quantidades maiores de compostos podem ter
efeitos opostos, em vez de inibir os efeitos tóxicos dos venenos; uma ação estimulante
pode ocorrer ou até mesmo produzir toxicidade e efeitos indesejáveis nas vítimas.
Além disso, a composição química das plantas varia de acordo com as
estações, o que sem dúvida influencia as propriedades biológicas e farmacológicas
das plantas (Pott et al., 2020). Os dados empíricos são corroborados pelo estudo de
(Yildiz et al ., 2024) usando o método LC -MS/MS, que revelou a presença de

85

numerosos polifenóis nos extratos de MO, incluindo isoquercitrina, que atua como
inibidora das atividades PLA s2 e hemorrágicas dos venenos de B. jararacussu e B.
neuwiedi (Vale et al., 2011.); enquanto para a astragalina não há evidência científica
como antiveneno. No entanto, como mencionado anteriormente, a astragalina é um
composto bioativo de plantas com vários efeitos benéficos para os humanos (Kangra
et al., 2025.).
Vale notar que os trabalhos que descrevem os efeitos antiofídicos das plantas
não analisaram o conteúdo de polifenóis, assim como os venenos de serpentes
podem sofrer variação na composição química. Assim, comparar dados da literatura
com o presente trabalho é um desafio, incluindo o período de coleta das plantas e dos
venenos de serpente, bem como os fatores bióticos e abióticos. Além disso, o uso de
solventes para preparar extratos de plantas pode alterar sua composição química e,
por sua vez, pode alterar a eficácia inibitória das plantas.
Além dos componentes mencionados anteriormente, o extrato de MO tem
quantidades significativas de luteolina- 7-glicosídeo (28,83 mg/kg), apigenina- 7-O-
glicosídeo (3,33 mg/kg) e acacetina (2,28 mg/kg), bem como traços de hiperosídeo,
rutina e ácidos rosmarínico e chicórico. Nossa pesquisa confirmou ainda que o extrato
MO é rico em flavonoides e ácidos fenólicos que têm potencial terapêutico (Liu et al.,
2018). Uma conclusão semelhante foi descrita por (Sheikh, 2017) , que descobriram
que os extratos metanólicos e aquosos de MO continham altas quantidades de
polifenóis. A literatura mostrou efeito antiveneno dos ácidos tânico e gálico (T. R. Costa
et al. 2021; Mahadeswaraswamy et al., 2011.), e estudos de docking mostraram que
a ação inibitória desses compostos pode ocorrer através da interação com
aminoácidos no sítio ativo da PLA2 e outros da região N-terminal (Toyama et al., 2022).
Além disso, os ácidos fenólicos têm características atraentes em contraste com o
antiofídico comercial, incluindo baixos custos de produção, facilidade de síntese, não
requerem refrigeração, são quimicamente estáveis e têm composição química estável.
Sowa-Borowiec et al . (2020) determinaram que os extratos de MO contêm
umbeliferona, ácido melilótico, cumarina, ácidos p-cumárico e o-cumárico, quercetina
e derivados de kaempferol (quercetina 3- ramnosil-(1–6)-galactosídeo 7- O-
ramnosídeo e kaempferol 3- galactosil-(1–6)-glicosídeo 7- O-ramnosídeo), de modo

86

que esta planta tem uma composição química intrigante e novos compostos
antiofídicos que valem a pena investigar mais. A composição mais rica em polifenóis
do extrato obtido por outros autores pode ser explicada pelos diferentes métodos de
extração e condi ções climáticas em que a planta cresceu (Sowa-Borowiec et al .,
2025).
O extrato metanólico de AH foi encontrado contendo 29,59 mg/kg de ácido 3,4-
di-hidroxibenzoico e 15,45 mg/kg de hiperosídeo. Este extrato foi também enriquecido
com ácido cumárico e apigenina- 7-O-glucósido. Devido a esses fitocomponentes
vitais, a castanha- da-índia tem sido usada como fitomedicina para prevenir e tratar
várias doenças (Çelik e Aslantürk, 2023). Os resultados obtidos pela análise do perfil
polifenólico são consistentes com os achados relatados por outros autores que
identificaram algumas classes de componentes, incluindo flavonoides, goma, fenóis e
saponinas (Felipe et al ., 2013; Liaqat et al ., 2022) . Os resultados da triagem
fitoquímica qualitativa mostraram que o extrato metanólico de AH contém fenóis,
taninos, flavonoides e saponinas, mas não alcaloides e antraquinonas (Çelik e
Aslantürk, 2023), e, como mencionado, tais compostos têm efeitos antiveneno (Simas
Pereira Junior et al., 2020).
A diferença no perfil de inibição entre as atividades de B. jararaca, B.
jararacussu e B. neuwiedi pode ser devida à variabilidade na composição do veneno
dessas espécies. Como visto na literatura, os extratos de AH e MO têm sido usados
mundialmente para tratar insuficiência venosa, problemas vasculares, feridas e
hemorroidas (Küçükkurt et al ., 2010) , e essa é uma questão favorável para
desenvolver medicamentos a partir de ambas as plantas. Um dos componentes mais
promissores do extrato AH é a saponina triterpenoide β- escina, que tem múltiplas
ações farmacológicas, como antit umoral, antiviral, anti -inflamatória e com menos
efeitos adversos e maior segurança do que outros compostos (Yunyu Wang et al .,
2023). Essas questões favoráveis levaram à aprovação das sementes de AH pela FDA
para uso clínico (Yunyu Wang et al., 2023). Além disso, é importante observar que as
plantas AH e MO são cultivadas mundialmente em uma ampla faixa de temperatura e
condições climáticas e têm sido usadas na medicina tradicional para insuficiência
venosa, e ambas as plantas estão incluídas na Farmacopeia Europeia (Shikov et al.,
2021).

87

Os extratos de AH e MO inibiram a atividade PLA2 dos venenos de B. jararaca,
B. jararacussu e B. neuwiedi, mas a atividade de B. jararaca foi a mais inibida, em
aproximadamente 60%. O percentual de inibição contra os venenos de B. jararacussu
e B. neuwiedi foi de aproximadamente 30% e, portanto, apesar de tais espécies terem
composições do veneno diferentes, uma inibição semelhante foi alcançada. As
enzimas PLA s2 causam efeitos tóxicos, como mionecrose, inflamação, edema,
distúrbios na coagulação sanguínea e hemólise, que sem dúvida contribuem para os
sintomas tóxicos locais e sistêmicos d o envenenamento. Assim, o bloqueio dessas
enzimas dos venenos pelos extratos de AH e MO deve ser considerado.
A atividade anti-inflamatória do extrato de MO foi observada anteriormente em
ratos injetados com óleo de terebintina, que é um terpeno volátil isolado de pinheiros
(Pleşca-Manea et al., 2002). Os autores observaram que o efeito anti -inflamatório de
M. officinalis ocorreu pela redução tanto da ativação de fagócitos circulantes quanto
da produção de citrulina. Isso está de acordo com o efeito inibitório de AH e MO contra
a atividade PLA2 dos venenos de Bothrops spp. e, assim, as plantas podem ter ação
complementar no processo inflamatório que ocorre no envenenamento (Pleşca-
Manea et al., 2002).
O conhecimento sobre a composição química dos extratos de AH e MO é
extremamente importante para desenvolver novos compostos antiveneno a partir
dessas plantas. Como demonstrado neste trabalho, AH e MO possuem compostos
que atuam como inibidores de toxinas dos venenos de Bothrops spp. e, assim,
poderiam ser usados juntamente com o antiveneno comercial quando este tratamento
não estiver disponível ou for insuficiente. Assim, até onde sabemos, o presente
trabalho descreve pela primeira vez os efeitos inibitór ios dos extratos de AH e MO
sobre as atividades tóxicas in vitro causadas pelos venenos de B. jararaca, B.
jararacussu e B. neuwiedi, embora o mecanismo de ação não tenha sido abordado. O
isolamento dos compostos ativos das plantas e testes tóxicos adicionais in vivo dos
venenos (como hemorragia, edema, letalidade e miotoxicidade) são necessários para
compreender a eficácia e considerar essas plantas como tratamento complementar
para o envenenamento causado por essas serpentes endêmicas brasileiras. No
entanto, esses objetivos têm limitações, uma vez que os venenos de Bothrops spp.
são uma mistura de enzimas ativas com múltiplas isoformas e, portanto, avaliar os

88

efeitos neutralizantes dos extratos de AH e MO contra tais alvos será um longo
caminho a percorrer.

89

5. CONCLUSÃO

No presente estudo observou- se que os extratos de Aesculus hippocastanum
e Melilotus officinalis demonstraram atividade inibitória significativa in vitro contra os
venenos de B. jararaca e B. neuwiedi, embora tenham apresentado menor eficácia
frente ao veneno de B. jararacussu, evidenciando a influência da variabilidade
interespécies na composição dos venenos. A diversidade química dos extratos,
especialmente o conteúdo de flavonoides, ácidos fenólicos e saponinas, parece
desempenhar papel central na neutralização das toxinas, ainda que a eficácia não
esteja diretamente relacionada à maior concentração isolada de determinados
compostos.
Em conjunto, os dados obtidos fornecem respaldo científico para o uso
tradicional dessas plantas e indicam seu potencial como fontes promissoras de
compostos bioativos com aplicação no desenvolvimento de terapias complementares
ao antiveneno. No entanto, estudos adicionais envolvendo o isolamento de princípios
ativos, a elucidação dos mecanismos de ação e a avaliação in vivo são necessários
para melhor compreender sua eficácia e viabilidade terapêutica frente ao
envenenamento botrópico.

90

CONCLUSÃO GERAL

Os resultados observados nesta tese demonstram que produtos naturais
constituem fontes relevantes de moléculas com potencial antiveneno frente aos efeitos
tóxico-farmacológicos induzidos por venenos de serpentes do gênero Bothrops . Os
extratos de plantas e polissacarídeos sulfatados testados inibiram a proteólise,
coagulação e fosfolipase A₂ dos venenos de B. jararaca, B. jararacussu e B. neuwiedi.
As diferentes classes de metabólitos atuam sobre alvos comuns dos venenos
por mecanismos distintos e complementares. Compostos fenólicos, flavonoides e
taninos presentes nas plantas interagem com proteínas e podem quelar íons
metálicos, contribuindo para a inibição de metaloproteinases e serinoproteases,
enquanto polissacarídeos sulfatados atuam por interações eletrostáticas com as
toxinas, modulando sua atividade enzimática. A variação na eficácia entre os
compostos avaliados reforça a influência da origem e da estrutura química na
capacidade de neutralização das toxinas, destacando a diversidade metabólica como
fator determinante para a atividade biológica observada.
Em conjunto, os resultados confirmam que metabólitos de plantas e polissacarídeos
de algas e microalgas apresentam atividade antiveneno significativa, atuando em
diferentes etapas do envenenamento e se destacando como candidatos promissores
para uso como agentes auxiliares à soroterapia, especialmente no controle dos efeitos
locais. Esses achados reforçam o potencial biotecnológico dos produtos naturais e
sustentam sua relevância no desenvolvimento de novas abordagens terapêuticas
capazes de ampliar a eficácia do tratamento dos envenenamentos por serpentes do
gênero Bothrops.

ABSTRACT
Ethnopharmacological relevance: Snakebite envenomation (SBE) is the world’s most lethal neglected tropical
disease. Bothrops jararaca is the species that causes the greatest number of SBEs in the South and Southeastern of
Brazil. The main symptoms are local (inflammation, edema, hemorrhage, and myonecrosis) and systemic
(hemorrhage, hemostatic alterations with consumptive coagulopathy, and death) effects. Species of the genus
Siparuna, Siparunaceae, are used in folk and traditional medicine to treat SBE. However, limited information is
available concerning Brazilian Siparuna species against SBE.
Aim of the study: To investigate the correlation between the compounds present in the extracts of five Siparuna
species as potential agents against proteolytic activity, plasma coagulation, and phospholipase A2 (PLA2) activity
caused by B. jararaca venom, using data obtained by UHPLC-MS/MS, biological activity, and multivariate
statistics.
Materials and methods: The ethanol extracts from leaves of S. ficoides, S. decipiens, S. glycycarpa, S. reginae, and
S. cymosa were fractionated by liquid-liquid extraction using different solvents of increasing polarity (hexane,
dichloromethane, ethyl acetate, and n-butanol), affording their respective extracts, totaling 25 samples that were
assayed through in vitro plasma coagulation and proteolytic activity assays. Moreover, the extracts were analyzed
by UHPLC-MS/MS, using electrospray ionization (ESI) and atmospheric-pressure chemical ionization (APCI) in
negative and positive ionization modes. The data was processed in MZmine v. 2.53 and evaluated by multivariate
statistical tests (PLS) using the software UnscramblerX v. 10.4. These data were also used to build molecular
networks (GNPS), and some ions of interest could be annotated using the library of molecules on the GNPS
platform.

Results: A total of 19 extracts inhibited B. jararaca-induced plasma coagulation, with emphasis on S. cymosa and
S. reginae (800 s). The inhibition of the proteolytic activity was also promising, ranging from 16% (S. glycycarpa)
to 99% (S. cymosa, S. decipiens, and S. reginae). In addition, most extracts from S. cymosa and S. reginae inhibited
70–90% of PLA2 activity. Based on data from positive mode APCI analyses, it was possible to obtain a statistic
model with reliable predictive capacity which exhibited an average R2 of 0.95 and a Q2 of 0.88, indicating a
robust fit. This process revealed five ions, identified as the alkaloids: coclaurine (1), stepholidine (2) O-meth-
ylisopiline (3), nornantenine (4) and laurolitsine (5). This is the first study to evidence the potential antivenom of
alkaloids from Siparuna species.
Conclusions: Altogether, our results give support to the popular use of Siparuna extracts in SBE accidents, sug-
gesting their potential as an alternative or complementary strategy against envenoming by B. jararaca venom.
The predicted ions in the chemometric analysis for the assayed activities can also be correlated with the blocking
activity and encourage the continuation of this study for possible isolation and testing of individual compounds
on the used models.
1. Introduction
Snakebite envenomation (SBE) is an important public health chal-
lenge worldwide, being included in the list of neglected tropical diseases
by the World Health Organization (WHO). It is estimated to affect close
to 2.7 million people globally every year, especially in rural areas of
tropical and subtropical countries (Binorkar and Jani, 2012; Feitosa
et al., 2015; Adri˜ao et al., 2022). According to an estimate of WHO,
around 100,000 people annually die and 400,000 suffer disability due to
SBE (Scheneider et al., 2021a; Liaqat et al., 2022).
Most snakebite cases occur in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. Brazil,
with its large forest areas and great variety of venomous snakes, is
among the countries with the highest risk of SBE in South America, with
about 26,000–29,000 cases per year, followed by Venezuela (7,000),
Colombia (3,000), Ecuador (1,500), Peru (1,500), and Bolivia (1,000)
(Roriz et al., 2018; Scheneider et al., 2021a, 2021b).
Species of the genus Bothrops are responsible for 90% of the SBE in
Latin America. Most of the Brazilian snakebite accident notifications are
related to specimens of the Viperidae family, which comprise the genera
Bothrops (known as ‘jararaca’) (83.3%), followed by Crotalus (‘cascavel’)
(8.5%), and Lachesis (‘surucucu-pico-de-jaca’) (3.4%). In the Elapidae
family, the genus Micrurus (true ‘coral’) is responsible for 0.8% of these
accidents (Feitosa et al., 2015; Farias et al., 2018; Scheneider et al.,
2021a; Konrath et al., 2022). Clinical manifestations of bothropic acci-
dents are characterized by prominent local and systemic effects in the
victims, such as inflammation, edema, hemorrhage, renal or cardiac
failure, muscle necrosis, and eventually death (Otero et al., 2000; Jorge
et al., 2017).
Bothrops jararaca (Wied-Neuwied, 1824) is the species that causes
the greatest number of snakebites in South and Southeastern Brazil,
around 60% in areas at sea level as well as over 1000 m altitude, or even
in large cities (Moura et al., 2015; Machado et al., 2016; Jorge et al.,
2017; Farias et al., 2018). The venom of B. jararaca is a mixture of active
protein and peptides, including snake venom metalloproteinases
(SVMPs), snake venom serine proteinases (SVSPs), phospholipases A2
(PLA2), L-amino acid oxidases (LAAOs), hyaluronidases, and bradykinin
potentiators among others, and some of them are responsible for the
most toxic activities (Kisaki et al., 2021).
The treatment recommended by WHO and the Ministry of Health of
Brazil is performed by the intravenous injection of commercial anti-
venoms that are produced by hyperimmunization of equines. Antivenom
has been available for 120 years and is highly effective in preventing
mortality, especially if administered early in an adequate dose (Este-
vao-Costa et al., 2016). However, the utilization of antivenoms to treat
morbidity and disability as consequences of snakebites has been limited
by multiple factors, including adverse effects profile (fever or anaphy-
lactic shock), stringent storage conditions, specificity issues, risk of
immunological reactions, and high cost of production (F´elix-Silva et al.,
2017; V´asquez et al., 2013; Liaqat et al., 2022).
The inefficacy of antivenoms to neutralize the local effect of SBE may
have serious consequences for recovery of victims, affecting the quality
of life. Thus, seeking alternative treatments for SBE deserves deeper
investigation. Over the years, many attempts have been made to find
snake venom’s antagonists from plants, since these organisms produce
many compounds with unique and intriguing chemical structure. Some
of these compounds may be useful as supplement or alternative treat-
ments of SBE, and with less adverse events, better tolerability, and safety
profile (Binorkar and Jani, 2012; F´elix-Silva et al., 2017). The phyto-
chemical analysis of various plants has revealed that phenols, alkaloids,
triterpenoids, and steroids possess promising effects against the toxic
activities caused by snake venom (Janardhan et al., 2014; Singh et al.,
2017; Liaqat et al., 2022).
Currently, modern mass spectrometry techniques are widely
employed for the identification and structural analysis of compounds in
complex mixtures (Popov et al., 2022). In parallel, Computer-Aided
Drug Design has emerged as a pivotal method for integrating the intri-
cate complexities of biological systems with the predictive power of
computational algorithms (Khan et al., 2020; Mostofa et al., 2023; Niazi
and Mariam, 2024). Utilizing this data, fingerprint analysis can forecast
which metabolites are likely contributors to specific biological activities
even before isolating the target compounds. This approach complements
experimental analysis and aids in the rational design of novel thera-
peutic agents (Darwish et al., 2022; Sweilam et al., 2022).
Siparuna species, Siparunaceae family, thrive in the tropical and
subtropical regions of the Southern hemisphere. These plants hold sig-
nificance in folk and traditional medicine due to their therapeutic
properties, as evidenced by documented use in treating various illnesses
(Leit˜ao et al., 1999, 2000; Silva et al., 2021). In remote areas where
access to prompt medical care is limited, patients often experience
exacerbated conditions, leading to fatalities. Such circumstances prompt
at-risk populations to develop community-based solutions to address
their healthcare needs. For instance, in indigenous communities in
Colombia, macerated leaves of Siparuna gesnerioides (Kunth) A.DC. are
utilized to combat SBE (V´asquez et al., 2013, 2015; F´elix-Silva et al.,
2017), while decoctions or macerations of leaves, branches, and stems of
Siparuna thecaphora (Poepp. & Endl.) A.DC. are employed in the form of
drinks, external baths, and poultices to prevent SBE-related hemor-
rhaging (Otero et al., 2000; Gomes et al., 2010; Binorkar and Jani,
2012). Moreover, marginalized communities in the Amazon region of
Brazil commonly rely on Siparuna apiosyce (Mart.) A.DC., (synonym:
Siparuna brasiliensis), Siparuna guianensis Aublet and Siparuna ficoides S.
S. Renner and Hausner, locally known as ‘Lim˜ao bravo’, ‘Negramina’,
and ‘Yekuna’ respectively, in traditional medicine to mitigate the effects
of snake bites (Leit˜ao et al., 2000; Renner and Hausner, 2005; Rieder,
2013).
Based on these reports of Siparuna species against snakebite, and
given the lack of identification of compounds in these plants responsible
for such antivenom effect, this study aimed to investigate the correlation

2. Materials and Methods
2.1. Plant material
Leaves of S. ficoides (SF), S. decipiens (SD), S. glycycarpa (SG),
S. reginae (SR), and S. cymosa (SC), were collected at Reserva Adolpho
Ducke/Manaus/Brazil, in August 2015. Voucher specimens are depos-
ited at Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas da Amazˆonia (INPA) herbarium
(Manaus, Brazil) under the registration numbers INPA: 269731, 269734,
269732, 269735, and 269733, respectively. The plants names (species)
have been checked with worldfloraonline.org and reflora.jbrj.gov.br
website, in February 2024. This work was authorized by the Directing
Council of Heritage (Conselho de Gest˜ao do Patrimˆonio Gen´etico, CGEN)
by the authorization Genetic A3C04CB.
Dried and ground leaves were extracted by percolation with ethanol
96 ◦GL. Part of the crude ethanol extract (CEE) was fractionated by
liquid-liquid extraction between water-methanol 7:3 (v/v) and hexane
(HEX), dichloromethane (DCM), ethyl acetate (EtOAc) and butanol
(BuOH), affording their respective extracts. This method was performed
according to Leal et al. (2021).
2.2. Venom of B. jararaca
Lyophilized B. jararaca snake venom was kindly supplied by Ezequiel
Dias Foundation, Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais, Brazil. The venom was
kept at � 20 ◦C, and then dissolved in physiological saline at 1 mg/mL
concentration to perform the toxic assays. Snake venom collection was
conducted under the authorization of the Brazilian National System for
Genetic Heritage Management and Associated Traditional Knowledge
(SISGEN), process number A39CTRI 04E.
2.3. Antiproteolytic activity of Siparunas extracts
Proteolytic activity of B. jararaca venom was determined according
to the method of Garcia et al. (1978), using azocasein as substrate (0.2%,
w/v, in 20 mM Tris-HCl, 8 mM CaCl2, pH 8.8). Aliquots of B. jararaca
venom (5–50 μg mL� 1) were incubated with 0.4 mL azocasein at 37 ◦C
for 90 min in a total volume of 1.2 mL. The enzymatic reaction was
stopped by the addition of trichloroacetic acid (5%, v/v, final concen-
tration). The tubes were centrifuged at 15,000 rpm for 2 min and the
supernatant was removed and mixed with 2N NaOH. After 10 min, tubes
were read at the absorbance of 420 nm. An Effective Concentration (EC)
was defined as the amount of venom (μg.mL� 1) able to produce a vari-
ation of approximately 0.2 OD units at 420 nm. For inhibition experi-
ments, one EC of B. jararaca venom (24 μg mL� 1) was incubated for 30
min at 25 ◦C with the Siparuna extracts (240 μg mL� 1), saline (S) or with
0.9% DMSO (DM), final concentration. Then, an aliquot of each mixture
was added to medium reaction, and proteolytic activity was performed,
as described. The negative controls of such activity contained solely the
Siparuna extracts or solvents, in the absence of venom. Then, the anti-
proteolytic activity was determined.
2.4. Anticoagulant activity of Siparunas extracts
A pool of citrated normal human plasma (diluted with an equal
volume of saline) from healthy volunteers of the hospital of Federal
Fluminense University (UFF) was mixed with B. jararaca venom (2.5–70
μg mL� 1) and the coagulation time was assessed using a digital coa-
gulometer (Amelung, model KC4A, Labcon, Germany). The concentra-
tion of venom (20 μg mL� 1) able to clot plasma approximately in 60 s
was designated as the minimum coagulant concentration (MCC). To
evaluate the inhibitory effect of the plant, Siparuna extracts (200 μg
mL� 1) were incubated for 30 min at 25 ◦C with one MCC of venom (20
μg mL� 1) or with saline or with 0.9% DMSO, final concentration. Then,
an aliquot of each mixture was added to plasma and coagulation time
was registered in the coagulometer. The negative controls were per-
formed in parallel by mixing Siparuna extracts or solvents with plasma,
in the absence of B. jararaca venom.
2.5. Antiphospholipase A2 activity of Siparunas extracts
PLA2 activity of B. jararaca venom was measured according to
Marinetti (1965) and Castro-Pinheiro et al. (2024). B. jararaca venom
(40 μg mL� 1) was incubated with solvents (saline or 0.9% DMSO) or
with Siparuna extracts (400 μg mL� 1) for 30 min at 25 ◦C, and then an
aliquot of this mixture was added to medium containing 580 μL saline,
25 μL sodium taurocholate 0.4%, 25 μL Tris-HCl (200 mM), pH 7.5, 20
μL CaCl2 (0.5 M). The enzymatic reaction was initiated by the addition
of the egg yolk substrate, and after 30 min of reaction at 37 ◦C, the tubes
were read at the absorbance of 740 nm. PLA2 activity (100%) of the
venom was determined using venom incubated with solvents in the
absence of Siparuna extracts, and negative controls of PLA2 activity
contained only solvents (saline and DMSO).
2.6. Statistical analysis
Results are presented as means ± S.E.M. The statistical significance
of variance using ANOVA and Dunnett post-hoc were performed using
GraphPad Prism® software. P values of <0.05 were considered statis-
tically significant.
2.7. UHPLC-MS/MS analysis
The extracts (2 μg mL� 1) were analyzed in a UHPLC Dionex Ultimate
3000 (ThermoFischer Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) coupled to a
LCQfleet (ThermoFischer Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The analyzes
were performed using a Acquity BEH C18 column (1.7 μm, 2.1 × 100
mm, 100 Å) with a flow rate of 0.45 mL min� 1 according to the elution
gradient: (0 min, 5%B), (20 min, 95%B), (25 min, 95%B), (31 min,
100%B), (37 min, 95%B) and (5 min, 0%B). The mass spectrometer,
equipped with atmospheric pressure chemical ionization (APCI) and
electrospray (ESI) was operated in positive and negative ionization
modes. MS spectra were acquired with a range of m/z 100–1000 and the
normalized collision energy of the collision-induced dissociation (CID)
cell was set at 35 eV.
2.8. Chemometric and molecular networking analysis
The LC-MS/MS data were converted to the.mzML format using the
Proteowizard toolkit (MSConvert v. 3.02) and processed utilizing
MZmine v. 2.53. Subsequently, the MZmine results were uploaded to the
Global Natural Products Social Molecular Networking (GNPS) online
platform, together with the openly accessible converted files (.mzML)
and metadata table. Default standards for unity resolution data were
applied for both data mining and molecular network construction pro-
cesses. The molecular network data were then downloaded and analyzed
in Cytoscape v. 3.9.1. The processed chemical and biological data were
exported to UnscramblerX software version 10.4.

3. Results and discussion
Plant extracts are widely used in traditional medicine as therapy for
snakebite, and especially in tropical regions where plant resources are
diverse and plentiful (Nishijima et al., 2009; Carvalho et al., 2013;
Dellacassa et al., 2014; Oliveira et al., 2014). In this scenario, various
plant species are used as local first aid for treating snakebite accidents in
Brazil, and some of them can effectively inhibit lethality, neurotoxicity,
hemorrhage, and venom enzyme activities (Konrath et al., 2022).
Siparuna is recognized as the major and most complex genus of the
Siparunaceae family with several species with medicinal and econom-
ical interest. These plants produce a variety of bioactive compounds,
being flavonoids and alkaloids the most characteristic (Costa et al.,
2013; Leal et al., 2021). Previous investigations of extracts from plants
of this genus have reported antispasmodic, antitumoral (Renner and
Hausner, 2005; dos Santos et al., 2023), and antiviral activities (Leal
et al., 2021a; Leal et al., 2021b; Leal et al., 2022).
Based on traditional uses of plants of this genus to treat snakebites
(Leit˜ao et al., 2000; Renner and Hausner, 2005; Rieder, 2013), CEE from
the leaves of five Siparuna species (SC, SD, SF, SG, and SR) and their four
extracts obtained after liquid-liquid extraction (HEX, DCM, EtOAc, and
BuOH) were assayed against the proteolytic, coagulant, and PLA2 ac-
tivity of B. jararaca venom.
3.1. Antiproteolytic activity of Siparuna extracts
Fig. 1 shows that the inhibition of the Siparuna extracts on the pro-
teolytic activity of B. jararaca venom occurred with different inhibitory
percentages. The HEX extracts from SF, SD, and SG, as well as the CEE
and BuOH from SF did not inhibit proteolysis (Fig. 1); while all other
Siparunas extracts affected proteolysis from 30 to 96 %. Overall, it
seemed that the extracts of SF inhibited less the proteolysis caused by
B. jararaca venom, and SC inhibited more efficiently, near to 95%. The
DCM and EtOAc extracts from SD inhibited proteolysis with values of
90%, as well (Fig. 1).
All the lowest polarity hexane extracts of Siparuna species (except the
one from SC – 40% and SR – 34%) did not inhibit proteolysis. The ex-
tracts CEE, EtOAc, and BuOH from SG inhibited proteolysis at 50, 70,
and 80%, respectively. It is worth saying that only the five extracts from
SR (CEE = 59%, HEX = 34%, DCM, EtOAc, and BuOH = 85% each) and
SC (CEE = 94%, HEX = 40%, DCM = 48%, EtOAc, and BuOH = 96%
each) inhibited proteolysis; On the other hand, at least one or two ex-
tracts of SF, SD, and SG, failed to inhibit proteolysis caused by
B. jararaca venom (Fig. 1). All Siparuna extracts, in the absence of
B. jararaca venom did not hydrolyze azocasein, and, thus, were devoid of
proteolytic activity (data not shown).
Natural compounds like terpenes, phenolics, and alkaloids,
commonly found in medium and high polarity extracts (DCM, EtOAc,
and BuOH) constitute the predominant group of compounds that are
responsible for the inhibition of toxic activities of snake venoms.
Therefore, they may provide therapeutic molecular models against SBE
to supplement the conventional serum therapy or for the development of
a novel antivenom therapeutic (Samy et al., 2012; Carvalho et al., 2013;
Baraldi et al., 2016; Adri˜ao et al., 2022).
A study carried by Oliveira et al. (2016) showed that the extracts of
Erythroxylum ovalifolium Peyr. and Erythroxylum subsessile (Mart.) O.E.
Schulz, from where terpenes and flavonoids were isolated inhibited the
proteolytic activity of Lachesis muta (Lineu, 1766) venom, but with
different potencies. The DCM and BuOH extracts of E. ovalifolium and
aqueous extracts of E. subsessile inhibited more than 80% of the pro-
teolytic activity, while the CEE, EtOAc, and aqueous extracts of
E. ovalifolium, and the DCM extract of E. subsessile inhibited proteolysis
from 40 to 75%. In contrast, the HEX and EtOAc extracts of E. subsessile
inhibited proteolysis below 10%.
The DCM, HEX, and EtOAc extracts from the marine seaweed Plo-
camium brasiliense Grev. M. Howe & W.R. Taylor inhibited proteolytic
activity of B. jararaca venom, so that these extracts may be interacting
with proteases of such venom. In contrast, the extract of this seaweed
prepared in hydroalcoholic solution failed to inhibit proteolysis (Silva
et al., 2015). The fruit extracts (aqueous, methanol-MeOH, and acetone)
from Clusia fluminensis Planch & Triana exhibited the most prominent
antiproteolytic activity on proteolysis induced by B. jararaca venom,
followed by extracts from the stems (MeOH) and leaves (aqueous).
Moreover, the aqueous extract of the fruits of C. fluminensis inhibited
more efficiently the proteolysis caused by the venom of B. jararacussu
(da Silva et al., 2019; Faria et al., 2023).

3.2. Anticoagulant effect of Siparuna extracts
As shown in Fig. 2, most of the extracts inhibited plasma coagulation
induced by the venom of B. jararaca, except for the extracts from SF
(CEE, HEX, EtOAc, and BuOH), SG (CEE), SR (HEX), and SC (DCM).
However, the extracts CEE, EtOAc, and BuOH of SC fully inhibited
coagulation of plasma, since no plasma coagulation occurred during
800 s which was the maximal period of observation of coagulation
(Fig. 2).
Moreover, the five extracts from SD (CEE, HEX, DCM, EtOAc, and
BuOH), four extracts from SG (HEX, DCM, EtOAc, and BuOH) and three
from SR (DCM, EtOAc, and BuOH) inhibited plasma coagulation. On the
other hand, only one extract from SF (DCM) and SC (HEX) inhibited
coagulation (Fig. 2). Thus, these extracts from Siparuna would prevent
bleeding or vascular disturbances caused by B. jararaca bites and, un-
doubtedly the polarity of extracts interferes in the effectiveness of in-
hibition. All the Siparuna extracts, in the absence of B. jararaca venom
did not clot plasma, and, thus, were devoid of procoagulant effect (data
not shown).
This profile was also observed in a previous study by da Silva et al.
(2019), where the plasma coagulation caused by B. jararaca venom was
attenuated by the crude extracts of C. fluminensis; while the highest
anticlotting activities were recorded for acetone and MeOH extracts of
the stems of Clusia. The fruit (acetone, MeOH, aqueous) and flower
(HEX) extracts had similar anticlotting properties (da Silva et al., 2019).
Regarding the B. jararacussu venom-induced coagulation, the aqueous
extracts of the leaves, stems, and fruits of C. fluminensis inhibited
coagulation, as well (da Silva et al., 2019; Faria et al., 2023). Terpe-
noids, sterols, and phenolic compounds were isolated and identified in
the HEX and MeOH extracts of this species (Mazza et al., 2019; Camara
et al., 2018; Guimar˜aes et al., 2021).
The DCM, BuOH or water extracts of E. ovalifolium, as well as the
HEX, EtOAc, or DCM extracts of E. subsessile did not inhibit the coagu-
lation activity of L. muta venom. In contrast, the CEE or EtOAc extracts
of E. ovalifolium and the CEE, BuOH, or aqueous extracts of E. subsessile
significantly delayed plasma coagulation induced by L. muta venom.
Additionally, neither the extracts nor solvents induced coagulation of
plasma (Oliveira et al., 2016).
A study carried by Silva et al. (2015) showed that the DCM extract of
the seaweed P. brasiliense inhibited coagulation induced by B. jararaca
venom, preventing fibrin production. In contrast, the hydroalcoholic
extract failed to inhibit coagulation provoked by B. jararaca venom. The
studies with plants or seaweed extracts obtained with solvents of
different polarities, demonstrate the great chemical variety and broad
profile of biological activity of such extracts against proteolytic and
coagulant activities caused by snake venoms.
3.3. Antiphospholipase A2 effect of Siparuna extracts
The extracts from SF (HEX, DCM and BuOH) and SC (HEX) failed to
inhibit significantly PLA2 activity of B. jararaca venom. All extracts from
SD, as well as the extracts from SF (CEE and EtOAc), and SR (HEX)
inhibited 30%–40%. On the other hand, SG (CEE, HEX and DCM) and SC
(DCM) extracts inhibited around 60%, while those from SR (CEE, DCM,
EtOAc and BuOH), and SC (CEE, EtOAc and BuOH) inhibited 70–90%
the PLA2 activity of B. jararaca venom (Fig. 3). These results corroborate
what was previously observed for the anticoagulant and antiproteolytic
activities of S. cymosa and S. reginae, highlighting their EtOAc and BuOH
extracts.
The literature widely acknowledges that snake venoms comprise a
complex blend of active proteins and peptides, particularly the families
of SVMPs, SVSPs, and PLA2, which elicit a wide range of toxic effects
such as disrupting blood coagulation, hemolysis, edema and muscle
necrosis (Leit˜ao et al., 1996; Kisaki et al., 2021). Previous works with
antivenom plant extracts also address inhibition of PLA2 as target. Ex-
tracts from leaves of Azima tetracantha Lam. (Petroleum ether, HEX,
chloroform, EtOAc, MeOH, and water) (100 μg mL� 1) rich in flavonoids,
phytosterols and proteins, were tested against different toxic enzymes
from the venoms of Bungarus caeruleus (Scheneider, 1801) and Daboia
russelli (Shaw & Nodder, 1797), where chloroform and EtOAc extracts
showed B. caeruleus PLA2 inhibition of 81% and 61%, respectively
(Janardhan et al., 2014). Kusar et al. (2024) analyzed anti-snake venom
potential (Naja naja) of Vitex negundo L. root extracts, through various in
vitro assays targeting the PLA2 enzyme. The results demonstrated that all
extracts effectively neutralized the hydrolytic action of phospholipases,
with inhibition values ranging between 59.83% and 69.33%, with IC50
values ranging from 0.278 mg/mL (for MeOH) to 0.392 mg/mL (for
DCM). These results corroborate our findings, which indicate better
activities for the medium and high polarity fractions.
The investigation of extracts’ capacity to inhibit the proteases and
PLA2 enzymes found in snake venoms offer valuable insights into the
ability of these products to mitigate tissue degradation or disruptions in
the coagulation cascade, thereby reducing the risk of local hemorrhages
(Adri˜ao et al., 2022; Sampat et al., 2023). Furthermore, assessing their

potential to interfere with blood coagulation is crucial for determining
their efficacy in preventing or treating coagulopathies induced by

Previous studies with extracts derived from the leaves, branches, and
stems of S. techaphora demonstrated antihemorrhagic properties against
B. asper and B. atrox venoms (Otero et al., 2000; Lomonte et al., 2009).
However, this is the first study to investigate and demonstrate the
inhibitory potential of plasma coagulation, proteolytic, and PLA2 ac-
tivity of species within the genus Siparuna. The inhibition of such ac-
tivities is undoubtedly important to ameliorate the snake
venom-induced hemorrhaging in victims since SVSPs, SVMPs, and
PLA2 enzymes contribute to this toxic effect.
Particularly noteworthy are the inhibiting plasma coagulation, PLA2
and proteolysis percentages of SC (CEE, EtOAc, and BuOH), SD (CEE,
DCM, EtOAc, and BuOH), SR (DCM, EtOAc, and BuOH), SG (EtOAc and
BuOH), and SF (DCM) extracts, confirming the ethnomedicinal potential
of species within the genus against snake venom (Leit˜ao et al., 2000;
Renner and Hausner, 2005; Rieder, 2013). Previous studies conducted
by our research group led to the isolation and identification of flavo-
noids and alkaloids from the DCM and BuOH extracts of these species
(Leal et al., 2021a, 2021b, 2022). Recent studies highlight that these
classes of specialized metabolites have shown prominence in combating
the effects resulting from the bite of Bothrops species (Adri˜ao et al., 2022;
Sachetto et al., 2022; Torres et al., 2023).
Medicinal plant extracts are a result of the combined action of
multiple compounds with synergistic, additive, or antagonistic activity,
being necessary future research to determine if either the crude extracts
or the isolated compounds are more efficacious as antivenom (Fer-
nandes et al., 2018; Vaou et al., 2022). However, as known from liter-
ature, snake venoms are a mixture of active proteins or peptides, and, to
neutralize efficiently all these compounds is a difficult task and a
challenge.
In this context, the assessed extracts of Siparuna showcased a po-
tential to inhibit plasma coagulation, proteolysis, and PLA2 activity,
thereby mitigating the toxic effects of snake envenomation. Therefore,
conducting these in vitro assays is essential for pinpointing promising
compounds with therapeutic potential against both the localized and
systemic effects of snake venoms, ultimately facilitating the advance-
ment of more effective and safer treatments for individuals bitten by
snakes.
3.4. Chemometric analyses using the PLS regression model
To predict compounds potentially associated with the inhibition of
proteolytic and coagulant activities of B. jararaca venom, we conducted
a liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/
MS) analysis of the 25 extracts originating from the five Siparuna spe-
cies. The results of the anti-PLA2 activity were excluded from the che-
mometric analyses due to its statistical relevance compared to the
responses of other activities. PLA2 may be associated with coagulant and
proteolytic effects, being identified as one of the targets responsible for
the toxic effects of venom (Marcussi et al., 2007). This could lead to
redundancy in model responses or increase the statistical weight of one
of the targets (anticoagulant and antiproteolytic) already evaluated,
resulting in increased intrinsic errors and reduced robustness of the
multitarget model. Therefore, this assay was conducted solely to
investigate the possible mechanisms of action involved in the
venom-neutralizing activity of the investigated extracts. This analysis
employed two ionization sources, both in positive and negative modes
(LC-ESI/APCI-(+/� )-MS/MS). Furthermore, continuous values repre-
senting the antiproteolytic and anticoagulant activities of Siparuna ex-
tracts were also employed for chemometric analyses.
For the development of a correlation model, we established a Partial
Least Squares Regression (PLS) analysis, linking the LC-MS dataset of the
25 extracts as independent variables (X), with the dependent variables
(Y) representing the activities against the targets. This algorithm in-
tegrates principal component analysis (PCA) and linear regression, with
the aim of identifying latent variables that enhance the correlation be-
tween predictors (m/z ions) and biological activity.
We also modeled all four chemical datasets (data not shown), and the
data obtained from positive APCI ionization exhibited the highest
explained variance, R2 and Q2 values, as well as the lowest root mean
square error (RMSE) (Fig. 4A–B).
The PLS model achieved a calibration explained variance of 98.3%
using ten factors. The model exhibited an average R2 of 0.95 and a Q2 of
0.88, indicating a robust fit. Furthermore, it displayed low RMSE values,
with RMSECV (cross-validation error) at 0.29, slightly higher than
RMSEC (calibration error) at 0.19. This relationship of RMSECV >
RMSEC confirmed the representativeness of the calibration data and the
absence of overfitting in the model. Based on the PLS analyses, patterns
in the sample distribution were identified, allowing classification into
two groups based on average activity values across of the two activities:

3.5. Annotated compounds using molecular networking analyses
In natural products (NP) chemistry the use of advanced computa-
tional techniques is common to expedite the discovery of bioactive NP,
organizing and extracting insights from large datasets (Yang et al., 2013;
Silva et al., 2021; Gogoi et al., 2021). In this context, molecular net-
works are capable of successfully structuring extensive mass spectrom-
etry data and sample metadata, presenting them in a user-friendly visual
format known as spectral similarity networks (Pilon et al., 2021).
So after processing the UHPLC-APCI(+)-MS/MS data in MZmine,
they were analyzed on the GNPS online platform for the creation of
molecular networks. Several networks were formed, revealing the
chemical complexity of the extracts. The predicted ions could be iden-
tified within the highlighted network depicted in Fig. 5.
It is interesting to note that the predicted ions shown in the che-
mometric analyses for both evaluated activities (antiproteolytic and
anticoagulant) appeared prominently in more active species, SR and SC,
red and blue colors, respectively. It is also possible to notice the presence
of some of the predicted molecules in the extracts of SG and SD (purple
and yellow, respectively); however, these extracts did not inhibit pro-
teolysis and plasma coagulation caused by B. jararaca venom. This can
be explained either by the lower abundance (area signal) of these
compounds in these extracts, or by the absence of compounds with
higher activity, as well as a possible synergy among some of the pre-
dicted active molecules.
UHPLC-APCI(+)-MS/MS analysis of the extracts and MS/MS frag-
ments of predicted ions strongly suggest that they are alkaloids
(Table 1), already described in the literature for Siparuna species (Leit˜ao
et al., 1999; Leal et al., 2021a, 2022).
Data obtained in the positive ionization mode were effective in
pointing out alkaloids of the benzylisoquinoline (coclaurine-1), proto-
berberine (stepholidine-2), and aporphine classes (O-methylisopiline-3,
nornantenine-4, laurolitsine-5) (Fig. 6).
Compound 1 at m/z 286 [M+H]+ was annotated based on diagnostic
fragment ions (m/z 107 and m/z 192) and neutral losses (NH3 or
CH3NH2, H2O, CO, CH3OH) characteristic for the benzylisoquinoline
skeleton (Leal et al., 2022). Coclaurine has been previously reported in
dereplication studies by our group for S. glycycarpa, S. decipiens,
S. reginae and S. cymosa (Leal et al., 2021a, 2022). Concerning com-
pound 2, m/z 328 [M+H]+, MS/MS data showed typical fragments of
the protoberberine class of alkaloids mainly due to the presence of the
diagnostic fragment ion at m/z 178, formed via a retro-Diels-Alder ring
opening (Lima et al., 2020).
On the other hand, the compounds 3, 4 and 5, aporphine derivatives,
were annotated for m/z 312, 326 and 314 [M+H]+ based on their
fragmentation pattern, i.e, the initial losses of NH3 (� 17Da) or CH3NH2
(31Da) followed by CO (� 28Da) when an CH2O (� 30Da) followed by
CO there is a methylenedioxy group (compound 4), OH and an OCH3
group when are vicinal in the aromatic ring (compound 5) (St´evigny
et al., 2004).
Some of these compounds have already been described by our group
in BuOH extracts of Siparuna species through LC-MS/MS data like
compound 1 (SG and SC-originally identified as S. sarmentosa), com-
pounds 2 and 3 (SG), compounds 4 and 5 (SC-originally identified as
S. sarmentosa) (Leal et al., 2021a, 2022). In addition, compound 3 was
isolated from S. poeppigii (Marti et al., 2013), and compound 4 has
already been isolated from S. tonduziana (Lopez et al., 1990) and
S. guianensis (Simas et al., 2001).
Finally, compound 6 was not identified, but its fragmentation
pattern is like that of the benzylisoquinoline class. Additionally, it is in
the same network as the predicted ions, strongly suggesting that it is also
an alkaloid as the annotated compounds.
Alkaloids have numerous biological activities, but only a few reports
describe their inhibitory activities against the enzymes of snake venoms
(Adri˜ao et al., 2022). The glycosylated alkaloid benzopyranylpiper-
idinone (schumanniofoside) isolated from the stem bark of Schu-
manniophyton magnificum Harms (Rubiaceae) reduced in vivo the lethal
effect of Naja melanoleuca Hallowell, 1857 venom (Akunyili and Aku-
bue, 1986).
An indole alkaloid (12-methoxy-4-methyl-voachalotine) isolated
from the root bark of Tabernaemontana catharinensis A.DC. (Apoc-
ynaceae) inhibited 100% of the lethality of Crotalus durissus terrificus
venom, besides showing antimyotoxic activity. Furthermore, this com-
pound inhibited PLA2-like proteins from B. jararacussu (Batina et al.,
2000; Borges et al., 2023). Seven steroidal alkaloids isolated from leaves
of Solanum campaniforme Roem. & Schult. (Solanaceae) showed anti-
myotoxic, antihemorrhagic, and antinecrotizing activity after in vitro
incubation of the venom of B. pauloensis Amaral, 1925; Torres et al.
(2011); Torres et al. (2013).
The nitrophenanthrene carboxylic acid alkaloid (aristolochic acid),
found in roots of Aristolochia indica L. and stems of A. sprucei L. (Aris-
tolochiaceae) has been reported as a promising antivenom compound
against the venom of D. russelii, B. jararacussu, Bothrops asper (Garman,
1883), Bothrops pirajai Amaral, 1923 and Naja naja Laurenti, 1768
through the inhibition of edematogenic, myotoxic, and hemolytic ac-
tivities (Vishwanath and Gowda, 1987; Chandra et al., 2002; Fernandes
et al., 2015; Bhattacharjee et al., 2017). Noteworthy is the fact that
plants of the genus Aristolochia are also used in Brazilian Folk Medicine
to treat inflammation, asthma, different kinds of cancer, and snakebites
(Bhattacharjee and Bhattacharyya, 2013; Giovannini and Howes, 2017).
Berberine, an isoquinoline alkaloid obtained from the stem bark of
Cardiospermum halicacabum L. (Sapindaceae), was discovered to be a
PLA2 inhibitor of the venom of D. russelii (Chandra et al., 2011).

Piperine, a derivative of piperidine and the primary alkaloidal compo-
nent found in the flowers of Piper longum L. (Piperaceae), could serve as
an effective treatment for Russell’s viper snake bites (D. russelii, Viper-
idae). It may be applied both systemically and locally, demonstrating the
inhibition of lethality, hemorrhage, necrosis, defibrinogenation, and
edema (Shenoy et al., 2013).
Plant alkaloids showed activity against the toxic effects of snake
venom, being potential candidates as an auxiliary in antivenom therapy,
particularly when dealing with the local toxicity (Santhosh et al., 2013;
Konrath et al., 2022).
This is the first study to demonstrate the potential of alkaloids from
Siparuna species against proteolytic, coagulant and PLA2 activities of
B. jararaca venom, considered to be the most toxic effects of this species
of snake. This research supports the traditional use of Siparuna as an
alternative to treat snake envenoming (Leit˜ao et al., 2000; Renner and
Hausner, 2005; Rieder, 2013).
4. Conclusion
Our results showed that the EtOAc and BuOH extracts from S. cymosa
and S. reginae stood out for showing the best profile of inhibiting for
proteolysis, PLA2, and plasma coagulation caused by B. jararaca venom,
thus showing the ability of such species as potential alternative or
complementary treatment strategy against SBE. The predicted ions in
Siparuna extracts point alkaloids of the benzylisoquinoline, aporphine,
and protoberberine types with high antivenom potential, which may be
correlated to the observed activity. Therefore, such results encourage
the continuation of this study aiming the isolation of the pure com-
pounds and assay against proteolysis and coagulation. This is the first
report of the antivenom effect of these types of alkaloids.

Abstract
Snakebite envenomation is a neglected tropical disease and incidents of the pit viper Lachesis muta cause hemorrhage, mus-
cle damage, blood coagulation disturbances, and even death; the proteases and phospholipase A2 (PLA2) of snake venoms
contribute to such toxic effects. This work evaluated the inhibitory effect of commercial fucoidans from two species of brown
seaweeds Fucus vesiculosus (FVF) and Undaria pinnatifida (UPF) against the coagulant and PLA2 activity of Lachesis muta
venom and two purified enzymes, a thrombin-like enzyme and PLA2, denoted TLE–1 and LM-PLA2–I, respectively. Fucus
vesiculosus and U. pinnatifida fucoidans were incubated with L. muta venom and enzymes for 5 min at 37 °C, followed by
assays, including the plasma and fibrinogen coagulation, hydrolysis of the substrates of proteases (S–2238 and S–2288), and
hydrolysis of the substrate of PLA2 enzymes, NBD-PC. Fucus vesiculosus and U. pinnatifida fucoidans inhibited the plasma
coagulation of L. muta venom, but not the coagulation of TLE–1. However, both fucoidans fully prevented the coagulation
of fibrinogen caused by L. muta venom and TLE–1. Fucus vesiculosus and U. pinnatifida fucoidans inhibited 60% and 40%
hydrolysis of S–2238 of L. muta venom and TLE–1, respectively. Using the substrate S–2288, the fucoidans did not affect
the hydrolysis of L. muta venom and inhibited 40% of hydrolysis caused by TLE–1. Fucus vesiculosus and U. pinnatifida
fucoidans inhibited 40% and 20% of the PLA2 activity of L. muta venom and LM-PLA2–I, respectively. These two fucoidans
should be investigated as complementary or potential adjuvants for SBE inflicted by L. muta venom in more detail.

Introduction
Snake bite envenomation (SBE) is classified by the World
Health Organization (WHO) as a neglected tropical disease,
causing 2.7 million accidents, 100,000 deaths, and 400,000
disabilities annually worldwide; however, due of underre-
porting, the true numbers of these incidents are expected to
be 40% higher (WHO 2019). SBE is a public health issue
that mainly affects rural developing tropical, subtropical,
and impoverished countries such as Asia, Africa, and Latin
America (Gutiérrez et al. 2017; WHO 2019). The Viperi-
dae (pit vipers or vipers) is considered the most venomous
snake family of medical relevance in Latin America; and
Brazil has approximately 360 species that cause approxi-
mately 25,000 incidents a year, accounting for 99% of the
registered incidents (Roriz et al. 2018; SINAN 2018). In
Brazil, four genera of vipers are found, namely Bothroco-
phias, Bothrops, Lachesis, and Crotalus and among them,

the genus Bothrops accounts for 87% of SBE (Roriz et al.
2018; SINAN 2018). Despite having the lowest rate of SBE
(~ 1.5–2%), envenomation caused by the genus Lachesis, it
has the highest mortality rates among vipers, approximately
1%, mainly due to substantial venom delivered (averaging
168–552 mg per snake) (Sanchez et al. 1992; SINAN 2018).
Lachesis, commonly known as bushmaster, has four species
distributed within the forests of Central and South Amer -
ica. This genus is the longest among vipers of the Americas
reaching up to 2.65 m in length, has nocturnal habitats, and
unique that lay eggs, approximately 5 and 19 with an incu-
bation period of circa 70 days (Cañas et al. 2023) (Fig.  1).
Brazil has one species, Lachesis muta, that is found in the
Amazon and northern Atlantic forests from Ceará to Rio
de Janeiro. Given these areas have low population density,
incidents caused by Lachesis are rare (Magalhães et al. 2019;
Sachett et al. 2022). Recent studies based on high-resolution
genomics, venomics, and morphological and ecological fea-
tures recognized the Amazon populations as L. muta; while
the Atlantic Forest as L. rhombeata (Hamdan et al. 2024).
Lachesis muta venom comprises a mixture of active pro-
teins, peptides, and enzymes, which are responsible for a
wide range of pathophysiological effects. The symptoms and
signs of envenoming are characterized by local pain and
inflammation, tissue damage, blistering, hypotension, neu-
rotoxicity, heart and kidney failure, and systemic hemostatic
disturbances e.g., hemorrhage, incoagulable blood and even-
tually death. (Fig. 1d) In the Amazon region of some coun-
tries of South America, L. muta and B. atrox are the major
species of clinical importance, and responsible for most
SBE with similar clinical features (Sanchez et al. 2006).
In general, snake venom serine proteases (SVSPs), snake
venom metalloproteases (SVMPs), phospholipases (PLA2s),
hyaluronidases, L-amino acid oxidases (LAAOs) are a fam-
ily of enzymes highly associated with venom toxicity and
symptoms of SBE (Gutiérrez et al. 2017; Tasoulis and Isb-
ister 2023). Three kind of SVSPs are reported in L.muta
venom, including the fibrinogen-clotting (thrombin-like
enzyme) that is involved in incoagulable blood, fibrin(ogen)
proteolysis, and resembles at least in part the mechanism
of action of the enzyme α-thrombin (Diniz and Oliveira
1992). The second is the plasminogen activator (LV–PA)
that mainly affect several steps of the fibrinolytic system
through plasminogen activation (Sanchez et al. 2000) and
the last enzyme is the kallikrein-like (LV–Ka) that releases
bradykinin from kininogen and contribute to hypotension,
neurotoxic, and shock in human victims (Felicori et al. 2003;
Weinberg et al. 2004). Thus, the action of such SVSPs may
explain at least partially the pathophysiological effects of
SBE by bushmasters.
Among biologically active enzymes, snake venom throm-
bin-like enzymes (SVTLEs) and PLA2s deserve attention
since most prominent toxic effects are attributed to them
(Sampat et al. 2023; Srinivasan et al. 2024; Romanazzi
et al. 2025). SVTLEs and PLA2s are widely present in
snake venoms and can activate the blood clotting cascade
system, i.e., they cleave fibrinogen into fibrin and induce
platelet aggregation leading to clot formation (Romanazzi
et al. 2025). Some hemorrhage symptoms of SBE are due to
thrombosis and consumption of plasma fibrinogen (Sampat
et al. 2023; Romanazzi et al. 2025). At present, over forty
SVTLEs have been purified from snake venoms, and thirty

of which have their primary structure determined with key
amino acid residues of the catalytic site, including His57,
Asp102, and Ser195 (Castro et al. 2004). PLA2 enzymes
are a large family of enzymes found in mammalian tissues
and in animal venoms, including snakes and are classified
into several groups based on structural homology, disulphide
pattern, and catalytic activity (Suranse et al. 2022). Further-
more, the presence of several isoforms of svPLA2s reflects
the diverse set of pathophysiological actions on human vic-
tims (Suranse et al. 2022). The catalytically active (Asp49
PLA2s) and inactive (Lys49 PLA2s) svPLA2s have a central
role in victims of SBE, and are involved in disrupting the
cell membrane’s integrity, tissue damage, edema, inflamma-
tion, pain, hemolysis, blood clotting disturbances, and anti-
coagulation and cardiorespiratory arrest; thus, they contrib-
ute to overall venom toxicity (Križaj 2023). These enzymes
cleave phospholipids resulting in the formation of arachi-
donic acid and lysophospholipids that are responsible for
the above mentioned toxic effects (Srinivasan et al. 2024).
Despite being widely distributed in snake venoms, signifi-
cant variability of toxic activity, as well as primary, second-
ary and tertiary structures, are reported in SVTLEs (Castro
et al. 2004) and svPLA2s (Srinivasan et al. 2024). One basic
PLA2 (LmTX–I) and one acidic PLA2 (LM-PLA2–I) were
isolated from L. muta venom and some pharmacological and
physico-chemical features were described (Damico et al.
2006; Fuly et al. 2022).
According to the WHO and Ministries of Health of many
countries, heterologous antivenom is the only available treat-
ment for SBE (WHO 2019). Antivenoms effectively prevent
death but are less effective in protecting against muscle dam-
age leading to an increase of physical sequelae, including
amputations and disabilities (Camey et al. 2002). Moreover,
antivenoms are costly and take time to produce and they
may even cause fever or anaphylactic reactions. The effective
recovery of bite victims relies on early and timely adminis-
tration of such antivenoms (Isbister 2024). Therefore, seek-
ing alternatives against the toxic effects of venom would
greatly benefit the victims of SBE.
Oceans contain many living organisms able to pro-
duce a wide array of compounds with intriguing and
novel chemical structures, as compared to the terrestrial
environment (Abdelmohsen et al. 2025). A wide range
of beneficial effects have been attributed to extracts of
seaweeds, such as antiviral, antifungal, antidiabetic, and
others (Mayer et al. 2024; Bouafir et al. 2025); these out-
standing bioactivities have drawn attention of nutraceuti-
cal and pharmaceutical industries worldwide. In general,
seaweeds contain an array of compounds derived from pri-
mary (e.g ., proteins, lipids, and polysaccharides) and sec -
ondary metabolism (e.g. , flavonoids, terpenoids, alkaloids,
carotenoids, and polyphenols) (Bouafir et al. 2025). Brown
algae are a large group of multicellular algae of the class
Phaeophyceae with 1,500–2,000 species worldwide which
includes a wide array of morphologies and sizes (Mayer
et al. 2024). They are the most widely researched group of
macroalgae, due to the presence in high amounts of bio -
active molecules; various species are located in tropical,
temperate, and polar marine environments (Mayer et al.
2024; Bouafir et al. 2025).
The brown seaweed Fucus vesiculosus (i.e., Bladder -
wrack; Fucales) is geographically distributed in the North
Pacific and North Atlantic oceans, shores of Europe, the
Baltic Sea, Canary Islands, and Northern Russia. Fucus
vesiculosus has been used in traditional medicine to treat
symptoms of hypothyroidism, obesity, atherosclerosis, cir -
culatory system disorders, and menopause (Catarino et al.
2018, 2017). Undaria pinnatifida (Laminariales) is an inva-
sive species also known as “wakame” regularly used as food
and in traditional medicine of Asian countries, including
Japan, South Korea, and China (Wang et al. 2018; Cheong
et al. 2025). Fucoidans or fucose-rich sulfated polysaccha-
rides are derived from various brown seaweeds, such as U.
pinnatifida and F. vesiculosus; these sulphated polysaccha-
rides have low toxicity and many bioactivities have been
ascribed, including immunomodulation, antitumoral, anti-
viral, anti–inflammatory, neuroprotective effects anticoagu-
lant, and antivenom properties (Pozharitskaya et al. 2020;
Xing et al. 2023; Castro-Pinheiro et al. 2024). Depending on
the species from which an extraction has been made and the
extraction method used, fucoidans have molecular weights
(MW) from five to several hundred kDa with noted varia-
tions on the sugar composition, glycosidic bonds, branching,
and degree of sulfatation and such issues contribute to the
widespread biomedical application of fucoidans (Lomar -
tire and Gonçalves 2022; Abbas et al. 2025). The diversity
in structure and MW contributes to differences in bioac -
tivities and subsequent biomedical application of fucoidan
polysaccharide (Abbas et al. 2025). As such, there is no one
type of fucoidan and the term fucose-containing polymer
(FCP) is perhaps the most appropriate. Previous reports of
our research group have evidenced that FVF and UPF are
non-hemotoxic molecules and inhibitory ability of FVF and
UPF fucoidans against the proteolytic, plasma and fibrino-
gen coagulant, and PLA2 activities of Bothropus jararaca,
B. jararacussu, and B. neuwiedi venom. In order to con-
tinue assessing fucoidans as inhibitors, it is of great interest
assessing their potential to inhibit other crude venoms and
purified enzymes of pit vipers.
Thus, because of antivenom potential of such molecules,
the present work aimed to investigate the effects of com-
mercially available fucoidan polysaccharides from Fucus
vesiculosus and Undaria pinnatifida against the plasma and
fibrinogen coagulant activity and PLA2 activity of L. muta
crude venom and two purified enzymes, TLE–1 and LM-
PLA2–I which were derived from this venom.

Material and methods
Snake venom, purified enzymes, and materials
Lachesis muta lyophilized venom was kindly provided by
the serpentarium of Ezequiel Dias Foundation (FUNED),
Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais, Brazil. The venom was dis-
solved in saline solution at the concentration of 1 mg  mL−1
and stored at –20 °C prior to use. Snake venom collection
was conducted under the authorization of the Brazilian
National System for Genetic Heritage Management and
Associated Traditional Knowledge (SISGEN), process num-
ber A39CTRI 04E. The purified enzymes LM-PLA 2–I and
TLE–1 (at concentrations of 0.5 mg  mL−1) were isolated
from the L. muta venom, accordingly to Fuly et al. ( 1997,
2022) and Magalhães et al. (2003), respectively.
Fibrinogen was purchased from Sigma Chemical Co and
dissolved in saline solution concentration of 0.9% w/v to
a stock concentration of 4 mg  mL−1. Chromogenic sub-
strates S–2238 and S–2288 were bought from Chromogenix
(Italy) and dissolved in Milli Q water to make up a stock
solution of 4 mM. The fluorescent phospholipid substrate
acyl-NBD–phosphatidylcholine (18:1–06:0 NBD–PC, code
(810132P –1 mg) was purchased from Avanti Lipid Polar
(USA). Powder NBD–PC was reconstituted in 200 µL of
100% chloroform, dried in glass tube under a slow stream of
pure nitrogen gas (N2), and dissolved in a saline solution to
a concentration of 1 mg  mL−1. Tubes containing NDP–PC
were sonicated at 4 °C three times, at intervals of 1 min and
stored at –20 °C prior to use. All other reagents were of the
best analytical grades.
Fucoidan extracts
Fucus vesiculosus fucoidan (FVF) and Undaria pinnati-
fida fucoidan (UPF), batch number DPFVF2021001 and
DPGFS2019537 respectively were kindly supplied by
Marinova (Cambridge, Tasmania, Australia). These com-
mercial samples were produced using a proprietary aqueous
extraction method by Marinova with a purity grade of > 95%.
A stock solution of FVF and UPF of 10 mg  mL−1 dissolved
in a physiological saline solution was prepared and stored at
–20 °C prior to use. The mass and chemical compositions of
FVF and UPF have been elucidated as described in Castro-
Pinheiro et al. (2024).
Effects of FVF and UPF on coagulant activity of L.
muta venom and TLE–1
The coagulant activity of L. muta venom and TLE–1 was
measured using a digital Amelung coagulometer, model KC4A
(Labcon, Germany). 200 μL fibrinogen (4 mg  mL−1) or human
plasma were incubated in the coagulometer for 1 min at 37 °C
and aliquots of 50 μL containing different concentrations of L.
muta venom (5–50 μg  mL−1) were added to plasma or fibrino-
gen and the coagulation time was monitored in seconds (s).
The concentration of L. muta venom (μg mL−1) able to clot
plasma or fibrinogen at approximately 60 s was denoted as the
arbitrary unit minimum coagulant concentration (MCC). A
concentration–effect curve was not performed for TLE–1 due
to a limited availability of this enzyme. Thus, a single chal-
lenge concentration of TLE–1 that clotted plasma or fibrino-
gen was approximately 50 μg  mL−1. One MCC of L. muta
venom (7 μL, 30 μg  mL−1) or TLE–1 (11 μL, 50 μg  mL−1)
was incubated for 5 min at 37 °C with either saline solution
(positive control), UPF or FVF at the ratio of 1:10 venom-to-
fucoidan (wt/wt) ratio, in a final volume of 220 μL adjusted
with physiological saline solution. Then, an aliquot (50 μL)
of each mixture was added to a reaction medium containing
200 μL plasma or fibrinogen. Coagulation time was registered
as described above. Negative controls contained saline solu-
tion, FVF, or UPF, in the absence of venom or TLE–1. Each
treatment group was assessed in quadruplicate in two inde-
pendent replicates, yielding n = 8. The pooled human plasma
was obtained from the blood bank of the Hospital Universi-
tário Antônio Pedro (HUAP) under the authorization of the
Committee for Ethics in Experimentation (CEP-UFF, CAAE:
28,941,314.0.0000.5243).
Hydrolysis of chromogenic substrates S–2238
and S–2288
Hydrolysis of chromogenic substrates S–2238 and S–2288
was monitored via a microplate reader from Biotek Synergy
H1 Hybrid Multimode Reader (Agilent, USA), using Gen5
software. 1.8 μL of FVF and UPF samples (100 μg  mL−1)
were incubated with 6 μL L. muta venom (30 μg  mL−1) and
18 μL TLE–1 (50 μg  mL−1) for 5 min at 37 °C in a medium
containing 20 mM Tris–HCl, 150 mM NaCl, pH 7.5 in a
final volume of 180 μL. The enzymatic activity was trig-
gered by adding 20 μL of S–2238 and S–2288 (0.4 mM,
final concentration) and the hydrolysis of substrates was
monitored at the absorbance of 405 nm for 5 min at 37 °C.
Negative replicated controls were performed by adding
saline solution or fucoidans in the absence of venom and
TLE–1. The final volume of reaction mixture was 200 μL,
and each experimental group was assessed in triplicate of
two independent replicates, yielding n = 6.

Statistical analysis
Results were expressed as the means ± standard devia -
tion (SD) and analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by
Tukey´s post hoc test and graphs were constructed using
Graph Prism version 9.0. p < 0.05 were considered to indi-
cate statistical significance.
Results
Effects of UPF and FVF on the plasma and fibrinogen
coagulation
LACHESIS muta venom (30 μg  mL−1) mixed in saline
solution (positive control group) clotted the human plasma
(Fig.  2A, black columns), and fibrinogen (Fig.  2A, white
columns) at approximately 25 s and 10 s, respectively.
Incubation of L. muta venom with fucoidan UPF or FVF
(100 μg  mL−1) fully prevented the venom–induced coagu -
lation on fibrinogen over the entire period of monitoring
coagulation, which was 900 s (Fig. 2A, white columns). On
the other hand, in the plasma, the venom-induced coagula-
tion occurred at approximately 50 s in the presence of FVF
and UPF (Fig.  2A, black column); thus coagulation time
was delayed twice. As seen in Fig. 2B (black columns), FVF
and UPF (100 μg  mL−1) did not prevent plasma coagulation
of TLE–1 (50 μg  mL−1) but inhibited the coagulation of
fibrinogen caused by TLE–1 (Fig. 2B, white columns). The
clot formed by the action of TLE–1 on plasma was visually
softer than that formed by L. muta venom (data not shown)
and this difference may be related to inefficacy of TLE–1 to
activate the coagulation XIII factor which is responsible for
stabilizing the fibrin clot. As negative control, UPF or FVF
neither clotted plasma nor fibrinogen in the absence of L.
muta venom and TLE–1 under the experimental conditions
(data not shown).
Effects of FVF and UPF on hydrolysis of chromogenic
substrates
The chromogenic substrate S–2238 is specific for thrombin
and S–2288 is sensitive to a wide range of serine proteases.
These substrates have been used to detect the presence of
such enzymes in a medium, as well as to assess the effects
of inhibitors of thrombin-like enzymes and serine proteases.
As seen in Fig.  3, a total of 100% of activity on S–2238
(A,B) and S–2288 (C,D) was achieved with L. muta venom
(30 μg/mL) and TLE–1 (50 μg/mL). FVF and UPF inhibited
hydrolysis of S–2238 caused by L. muta venom (Fig.  3A)
and TLE–1 (Fig.  3B) with percentages of 38% and 54%,
respectively. On the other hand, FVF and UPF did not inhibit
hydrolysis of S–2288 caused by L. muta venom (Fig. 3C) but
inhibited 60% of such activity caused by TLE–1 (Fig.  3D).

research was specifically on the Bothrops genus of pit viper
snakes which are endemic to Brazil and other South Ameri-
can countries. A study conducted by Azofeifa et al. (2008)
and Angulo and Lomonte (2003) described antimyotoxic
effect of fucoidan extracted from F. vesiculosus against B.
asper venom and purified myotoxins. However, in the pre-
sent work, the antivenom effect of species-specific fucoidans
against the most lethal specie of Brazil, L. muta, as well as
two purified enzymes from this venom, the thrombin-like
enzyme TLE–1 and PLA2 (LM-PLA2–I) are described for
the first time. Undoubtedly, it is urgent to inhibit the toxic
effects caused by the major groups of venomous snakes that
are responsible for the highest death rates after enveno-
mation. The genera Bothrops and Lachesis are responsi-
ble for majority of SBE reported in Brazil (SINAN 2018).
This new approach of using specific fucoidans against L.
muta venom and purified enzymes opens up possibilities to
develop antivenoms against SBE by vipers and can also be
a step towards assessing the mechanisms of action against
the main toxic classes of enzymes, including SVTLEs and
PLA2s. TLEs and PLA2s have a pivotal role in the symp-
toms of SBE since they are myotoxic, hemolytic, and acti-
vate and/or inhibited platelet aggregation induced by col-
lagen, arachidonic acid, and adenosine diphosphate (Fuly
et al. 1997; 2022; Magalhães et al. 2003). As mentioned in
the introduction, SBE caused by L. muta venom produces
a wide range of toxic symptoms in victims and the purified
enzymes, TLE–1 and LM-PLA2–I significantly contribute to
the toxicity of L. muta venom. Thus, inhibition of the activ-
ity of such enzymes should be of great interest to relieve
local venom toxicity and aid commercial antivenoms to treat
victims of SBE.
In general, SVTLEs are glycoproteins and the carbo-
hydrate moiety of such a family plays an important role
on the catalytic activity, structural stabilization, and
interaction with substrates (Ullah et al. 2018). As throm-
bin, SVTLEs have unique structures, causing cleave of
the fibrinogen, they have a primary structure homology,
and contain key amino acid residues of catalytic site (as
Ser195, His57, and Asp102) (Ullah et al. 2018). Thrombin
has two positively charged regions i.e., the anion-binding
exosites I and II that are located at a certain distance from
the catalytic site of the enzyme (Fredenburgh and Weitz
2025). In general, exosites I is referred to interact with
fibrinogen, heparin cofactor II, and the blood proteins of
the coagulate cascade factors V and Va; while exosite II is
responsible for enzymatic activity of thrombin and interac-
tion with heparin (Fredenburgh and Weitz 2025). Moreo-
ver, some SVTLEs have been commercially used as medi-
cines, including Ancrod (Arvin™, Knoll, Ludwigshafen,
Germany) which is isolated from Calloselasma rhodos-
toma, Defibrase™ from B. moojeni , Reptilase™ from B.
atrox, Crotalase from Crotalus adamenteus, and a TLE
purified from Agkistrodon contortrix (Castro et al. 2004);
though the use of them as medicines has been discontin-
ued due to immunological reactions and high production
costs (Castro et al. 2004). Literature has described inhibi -
tion of thrombin and SVTLEs activity through chemicals,
such as phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF) that is able
to bind serine residue at position 182 of the active site
of such proteases (Vilca-Quispe et al. 2023). Some com-
mercial anticoagulants, including heparin and hirudin (a
leech-derived thrombin inhibitor) inhibit the procoagulant
effect of thrombin and SVTLEs either through binding to
exosites II or I, which do not block the enzymatic activity
(Troisi et al. 2021). The negatively charged structure of
heparin as well as the sulfate groups of it allows a very
strong interaction of this polysaccharide with thrombin
(Troisi et al. 2021; Chan et al. 2024). FVF and UPF have
negatively charged chemical groups within their struc-
ture, but different from heparin, they have high molecular
weight (Castro-Pinheiro et al. 2024). Despite having high
molecular weights, FVF and UPF (up to concentrations
of 1,500 μg  mL−1) are considered non-toxic molecules
through the hemocompability assays and thus, having
potential to the development of medicines (Castro-Pin-
heiro et al. 2024). Bothrojaracin, a C-type lectin isolated
from B. jararaca venom is another promising molecule to
be evaluated as an inhibitor since it interacts with exosite
I and allosterically inhibits the catalytic activity of throm-
bin measured by the cleavage of S–2238 (Zingali et al.
2005). As seen in the present work, FVF and UPF inhib-
ited the hydrolysis of S–2238 and S–2288 caused by the
purified TLE–1 with similar inhibitory percentages (60%).
Curiously, fucoidans were unable to inhibit hydrolysis of
S–2288 by L. muta venom and inhibited less hydrolysis
of S–2238 (38%). As seen in literature, SVTLEs are able
to hydrolyze such substrates and are inhibited by classi-
cal protease inhibitors, including PMSF and benzamidine
(Zaqueo et al. 2014). The negatively charged regions of
such compounds from different sources are crucial to inter -
act with thrombin and SVTLEs leading to an inhibitory
effect of the pharmacological effects and enzymatic activ -
ity of these enzymes (Fuglestad et al. 2012). Therefore, a
similar mechanism of action may be attributed to FVF and
UFP against TLE–1, due to the negative chemical groups
within their structures as evidenced in the work of Castro-
Pinheiro et al. (2024). Synthetic peptides based on the
chemical structure of their substrates and natural inhibitors
have been assessed to inhibit SVSPs from B. jararaca and
B. atrox venoms (Saladini et al. 2024), but without signifi -
cant results. Therefore, the polysaccharides FVF and UPF
have a negatively charged structure that would allow them
bind to cationic aminoacids (Castro-Pinheiro et al. 2024),
but a docking approach may be a valuable strategy for
future research to further investigate the structural-activity

As seen in this work, FVF and UPF inhibited the
PL
A2
activity of L. muta crude venom and purified LM-PLA 2-
I as assessed by using the commercial fluorescent lipid
substrate, NBD–PC.
PL
A2s enzymes have key aminoacid
residues, including His48, Asp49, Tyr52, Tyr73, and Asp99
that comprise the catalytic domain (Chioato and Ward 2003;
Salvador et al. 2024) as well as others that facilitate binding
to the phospholipids of cellular membranes. Divalent
Ca+2
is an essential cofactor to
PL
A2s exert their enzymatic activ-
ity (Castro-Amorim et al. 2023). One may speculate that
the inhibitory effects of fucoidan, against
PL
A2 occurred
due to the negatively charged structure, especially the sul-
fate groups, thereby allowing fucoidans to react with such
positively charged residues, including Ca+2. Varespladib, a
synthetic PL
A2 inhibitor was referred by the U.S. Food and
Drug Administration (FDA) as a drug for SBE, and its mode
of action occurs through binding to hydrophobic groove and
Ca+2–binding active site, thus inhibiting the toxic effects of
P
LA2s of different snake species, including bleeding, hemor-
rhage, neurotoxicity, myonecrosis, edema, and death (Lewin
et al. 2022; Salvador et al. 2023; Sampat et al. 2023). On
the other hand, Varespladib at lower concentrations inhib-
ited PL
A2 activity of L. muta rhombeata but did not inhibit
metalloproteases of this venom (Sampat et al. 2023). As a
strategy to increase effectiveness of antivenom, Varespladib
was mixed with some venom neutralizing antibodies as a
cocktail to rescue mice against lethality of Elapidae venoms
(Glanville et al. 2025 ). In general, molecules derived from
primary and secondary metabolites from specific plants and
seaweeds act against the toxic activities of snake venoms
through the chelation of metals, protein precipitation, or
interaction of amino acid residues of the active site, includ-
ing His48 and Asp49 (Sampat et al. 2023 ). Data from the
literature showed that FVF fucoidans are approved by the
FDA in the category of Food Ingredients as “Generally
Recognized As Safe” (GRAS); while UPF is sometimes
employed for thyroid disorders related to iodine deficiency.
However, due to its high iodine content, the use of this sea-
weed as supplement or herbal preparation should be taken
into account because of the possibility of adverse effects and
interactions with other medicines, including lithium carbon-
ate or antihypertensive drugs (Gras 2018; Citkowska et al.
2019). Although the mechanism of action of
PL
A2s is not
fully understood, FVF and UPF are promising inhibitors of
their enzymatic activities. Some classical inhibitors have
been reported, as p-bromophenacyl bromide (p–BPB) that
reacts irreversibly with His48 of enzymatically active
PL
A2s
(Fuly et al. 1997, 2022; Soares and Giglio 2003); however, it
is considered toxic to humans and thus patently not feasible
for medical use to treat SBE.
In many locations, SBE represents an occupational and
environmental disease and causes a significant ongoing neg-
ative economic impact to those communities which reside
mainly in impoverished and rural areas (Roriz et al. 2018;
Junkes et al. 2024). Moreover, physicological damages asso-
ciated with SBE are increasing and strongly affecting health-
care system and workers (Junkes et al. 2024). Therefore, spe-
cific fucoidan polysaccharides, as FVF and UPF may open
up a possibility for drug design or their use in combination
with existing commercial antivenom as inhibitors of SVSPs
and PL
A2s that are considered the most toxic of snake ven-
oms; thus, may contribute to the relief of toxic symptoms of
envenomation by L. muta venom thereby saving lives.
